Issued at 300 PM EDT Tue Oct 6 2026

Through Tonight...Truly a tale of two different weather patterns 
across east central Florida this afternoon. Light showers 
overspread northern portions of the area along with high cloud 
coverage that has prevailed through this morning and into the 
afternoon hours, resulting in limited convective development. What
deeper convection has managed to develop has generally struggled 
across these northern portions, and a continued spreading of light
showers is likely through the remainder of today. To the south, 
less cloud coverage has allowed for daytime heating and the 
development of the sea breeze, which has pushed inland slightly. 
Convective development has been ongoing as a result, with 
scattered showers and storms across the Treasure Coast and 
portions of southern Brevard. The scattered, deeper convection 
will continue through this afternoon across the southern half of 
the forecast area, spreading inland as outflow from convection 
pushes westward. This activity will continue to be capable of 
producing lightning strikes and gusty winds up to 45 mph cannot be
ruled out with the strongest storms. Activity across the south is
anticipated to gradually wane into the late evening hours, with 
the lighter showers likely overspreading the remainder of east 
central Florida as the stationary boundary remains draped across 
the peninsula. Some drier periods overnight cannot be ruled out.

An area of low pressure is forecast to begin developing along the
boundary off the east coast of Florida tonight. There remains a 
good deal of uncertainty between models and even individual model 
runs on where the low will develop and just how strong it will be.
A slight increase in northerly winds along the Volusia and 
northern Brevard coasts will be possible tonight, though the 
greatest winds are anticipated on Wednesday. Muggy conditions 
persist due to the deep moisture across the state, with lows in 
the low 70s.

Wednesday-Thursday...The stalled boundary draped across the 
Florida peninsula will remain in place through the middle of this 
week, maintaining a deep plume of moisture across east central 
Florida. PWATs are forecast to remain between 2-2.5" areawide, 
supporting numerous to widespread showers locally each day with 
PoPs generally ranging between 70-85%. Multiple rounds of showers 
are anticipated, increasing the potential for flooding when 
combined with the already saturated soils from prior rainfall. 
Broad rainfall accumulations up to 4" will be possible through 
mid-week, though any deeper convection could prompt higher totals 
in localized areas. A Marginal Risk (1 out of 4) of excessive 
rainfall encompasses all of east central Florida both Wednesday 
and Thursday. Storm development cannot be ruled out with activity,
but confidence in coverage remains low. The deep moisture and 
higher cloud coverage will limit instability across the area, with
warmer temperatures aloft also inhibiting deep convective 
development. Occasional lightning strikes will be possible at 
times and isolated gusts up to 45 mph cannot be ruled out within 
the strongest storms. Showers are forecast to linger through the 
overnight hours each day, though coverage may wane slightly 
overnight.

Along the stalled boundary, the low pressure forming off the 
eastern coast of Florida is anticipated to bring some increasing 
northerly winds and higher seas into Wednesday, primarily along 
the Volusia and northern Brevard coasts. Wind speeds of 15 to 20 
mph will be possible at times, with gusts up to 30 mph possible. 
The increasing winds and seas will also bring deteriorating beach 
conditions to the Volusia and northern Brevard coastlines, and a 
high risk of rip currents will be possible. Elsewhere, wind speeds
are forecast to remain generally below 15 mph. Temperatures will 
remain generally in the 80s through Thursday, with high moisture 
keeping conditions muggy. Overnight lows generally in the low 70s.

Friday-Tuesday (previous)...All eyes late week and into this 
weekend turn to the Gulf, where an area of low pressure is being 
monitored for tropical development. While the forecast remains 
uncertain, ridging over the central US looks to shift eastward 
Friday into Saturday, allowing the low to move ashore somewhere 
along the northern Gulf coast. Locally, this could mean little for
the overall pattern. While this system may be able to drag the 
stationary front northward, southerly flow over the Florida 
peninsula would maintain deep moisture over the area. Currently, 
rain chances remain above normal (60-80%) Friday and this weekend,
